{{Short description|Polynomial function in three variables}}
The '''Källén function''', also known as '''triangle function''', is a polynomial function in three variables, which appears in [[geometry]] and [[particle physics]]. In the latter field it is usually denoted by the symbol <math>\lambda</math>. It is named after the theoretical physicist [[Gunnar Källén]], who introduced it as a short-hand in his textbook ''Elementary Particle Physics''.<ref>G. Källén, ''Elementary Particle Physics'', (Addison-Wesley, 1964)</ref>

==Definition==
The function is given by a quadratic polynomial in three variables
:<math>\lambda(x,y,z) \equiv x^2 + y^2 + z^2 - 2xy - 2yz - 2zx.</math>

==Applications==
In geometry the function describes the area <math>A</math> of a triangle with side lengths <math>a,b,c</math>:
:<math>A=\frac{1}{4} \sqrt{-\lambda(a^2,b^2,c^2)}.</math>
See also [[Heron's formula]].

The function appears naturally in the [[kinematics]] of [[Special relativity|relativistic]] particles, e.g. when expressing the energy and momentum components in the [[Center-of-momentum frame|center of mass frame]] by [[Mandelstam variables]].<ref name="byckling1973">E. Byckling, K. Kajantie, ''Particle Kinematics'', (John Wiley & Sons Ltd, 1973)</ref>

==Properties==
The function is symmetric in permutations of its arguments, as well as independent of a common sign flip of its arguments:
:<math> \lambda(-x,-y,-z) = \lambda(x,y,z). </math>

If <math>y,z>0</math> the polynomial factorizes into two factors
:<math> \lambda(x,y,z) = (x-(\sqrt{y}+\sqrt{z})^2)(x-(\sqrt{y}-\sqrt{z})^2).</math>

If <math>x,y,z>0</math> the polynomial factorizes into four factors
:<math> \lambda(x,y,z) = -(\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{y}+\sqrt{z})(-\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{y}+\sqrt{z})(\sqrt{x}-\sqrt{y}+\sqrt{z})(\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{y}-\sqrt{z}).</math>

Its most condensed form is
:<math> \lambda(x,y,z) = (x-y-z)^2-4yz. </math>

Interesting special cases are<ref name="byckling1973"/>{{rp|eqns. (II.6.8–9)}}
:<math> \lambda(x,y,y) = x(x-4y)\,,</math>
:<math> \lambda(x,y,0) = (x-y)^2\,.</math>
